relevance_reason: First report of homozygous KIRREL1 mutations causing steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in two families, with functional studies.

findings.statement: Solanki et al. (2019) reported that homozygous mutations in KIRREL1, a slit diaphragm component, cause steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS), and concluded that KIRREL1 has an important role in modulating the integrity of the slit diaphragm and maintaining glomerular filtration function.
quotes: Herein, we describe two unrelated families with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with homozygous mutations in the KIRREL1 gene.
Thus, the KIRREL1 gene product has an important role in modulating the integrity of the slit diaphragm and maintaining glomerular filtration function.

findings.statement: Solanki et al. (2019) described a boy (A666_21) from a consanguineous family who was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome at age 5 years, was steroid-resistant at initial presentation, and was resistant to various immunosuppressive drugs, never achieving complete remission and having undulating proteinuria with only partial response; ACE inhibitor and ARB treatment was not beneficial, but renal function remained normal over 12.5 years of follow-up. Renal biopsy showed minor mesangial hypercellularity consistent with minimal change disease. A younger sister had periorbital edema and proteinuria, and extended relatives included 3 children with ESRD and 1 with nephrotic syndrome, but their genotypes were unknown. There were no extrarenal manifestations.
quotes: The patient A666_21 was diagnosed with NS at age of 5 years. He developed SRNS at his initial presentation and was resistant to different immunosuppressive drugs. He has never achieved a complete remission and remained having undulating proteinuria with partial response to treatment.
Nevertheless, his renal function remained normal all over the time, so he stopped his clinical visits after 12.5 years of follow up.
Presence of only minor findings of mesangial hypercellularity is consistent with minimal change disease on light microscopy (H&E staining).

findings.statement: Solanki et al. (2019) described a boy of Italian descent (B742_21) from a consanguineous family who was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome at age 14 years and was steroid-resistant at presentation. He had hypertension and achieved complete remission on tacrolimus, a calcium channel blocker, and ACE inhibitor, but over 4 years of follow-up developed progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD stage 2). Renal biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and electron microscopy showed extensive podocyte foot process effacement, increased mesangial matrix and mesangial proliferation. There were no extrarenal or syndromic features.
quotes: The patient B742_21 was diagnosed with NS at age of 14 years. He developed SRNS at his initial presentation.

During the course of treatment with Tacrolimus, CCB and gradual dose increase of ACE-I the patient succeeded a complete remission. However, over 4 years of follow up, he developed chronic kidney disease, which has continued to progress attaining CKD stage 2 at the time of this publication
Renal histology of individual B742_21 with KIRREL1 mutation shows focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (arrows) on light microscopy (MPAS staining).

findings.statement: By whole-exome sequencing and homozygosity mapping in 596 individuals from 406 families with SRNS, Solanki et al. (2019) identified homozygous KIRREL1 missense mutations in 2 individuals from unrelated consanguineous families (frequency 2/406, 0.4%). Both residues were conserved to zebrafish and lay within homozygosity peaks on chromosome 1.
quotes: we performed whole-exome sequencing (WES) and homozygosity mapping in a cohort of 596 individuals from 406 families with SRNS.

We discovered two homozygous missense mutations (p.Arg440Cys and p.Ser573Leu) of the KIRREL1 gene in two individuals of unrelated consanguineous families (A666 and B742) with SRNS. So the frequency of this gene would be (2/406), which is 0.4 %

findings.statement: In patient A666_21 with SRNS, Solanki et al. (2019) identified a homozygous p.Arg440Cys missense mutation in KIRREL1, located within the maximum NPL homozygosity peak on chromosome 1; the allele had a gnomAD minor allele frequency of 3.97 x 10(-6).
quotes: Whole exome sequencing identifies a homozygous mutation of KIRREL1 (p.Arg440Cys) that is positioned within the maximum NPL peak on chromosome 1 (arrowhead).

The mutated alleles causing mutations p.Arg440Cys and p.Ser573Leu appear to be very rare based on the reference data base gnomAD with a minor allele frequency (MAF) of 3.97×10−6 and a MAF of 7.87×10−4 respectively

findings.statement: In patient B742_21, of Italian descent, Solanki et al. (2019) identified a homozygous p.Ser573Leu missense mutation in KIRREL1 within the maximum homozygosity peak on chromosome 1. This variant had a gnomAD MAF of 7.87 x 10(-4), an allele frequency of 0.0011 in Europeans, and was found in the homozygous state in one gnomAD control; the authors suggested possible incomplete penetrance or variable expressivity but considered in silico, conservation and functional data conclusive of its impact.
quotes: Notably, the p.Ser573Leu, identified in a child of Italian descent and found mutated at the homozygous state in one control subject in GnomAD, has an allele frequency of 0.0011 in European populations, which is very frequent.
thus, there is a possibility of variable expressivity or incomplete penetrance for this variant
Within the maximum NPL peak on chromosome 1 (arrowhead), we identified a homozygous mutation in KIRREL1 (p.Ser573Leu).

findings.statement: Solanki et al. (2019) found that Flag-tagged KIRREL1 Arg440Cys and Ser573Leu mutants stably expressed in human podocytes mislocalized, with reduced membrane fraction levels and increased localization in Golgi, early endosomes and lysosomes compared with wildtype, suggesting trafficking defects; NPHS1 membrane localization was unaffected. Podocyte monolayers expressing the mutants showed significantly increased albumin flux, indicating impaired intercellular integrity.
quotes: the mutant KIRREL1 proteins were present in the membrane fraction at a significant low level.
Both KIRREL1 mutants showed increased localization at Golgi apparatus, early endosomes and lysosomes

In comparison to cells expressing KIRREL1 wild type protein, a significant increase in albumin flux (an indicator of increase in transepithelial permeability) was noted within 1 hour (p <0.01), with a further increase at 4 hours (p< 0.001)

relevance_reason: Functional and in vivo rodent study of Neph1 (KIRREL1). It localizes the protein to the glomerular slit diaphragm and shows that it interacts with nephrin and ZO-1, and that disrupting the interaction causes proteinuria. No patients or variants are reported.

findings.statement: Liu et al. (2003) used immunogold electron microscopy in rodents to localize Neph1 to the glomerular slit diaphragm. They showed that Neph1 interacted directly with 2 other slit diaphragm components, nephrin and ZO-1. Both native and recombinant Neph1 associated with each other as dimers and multimers. Neph1 bound nephrin through the extracellular segments, and this interaction was specific: neither protein interacted with P-cadherin. ZO-1 bound the cytoplasmic tail of Neph1 through its PDZ domains.
quotes: we localize the expression of Neph1 to the glomerular slit diaphragm by immunogold electron microscopy in rodents and describe its direct interaction with two other components of the slit diaphragm, nephrin and ZO-1
Both native and recombinant Neph1 associate with each other as dimers and multimers and interact with nephrin via their extracellular segments.
The interaction between nephrin and Neph1 is specific and not shared by either protein with P-cadherin, another integral slit diaphragm protein.

findings.statement: Liu et al. (2003) disrupted the Neph1-nephrin interaction in vivo by injecting rodents with combinations of anti-Neph1 and anti-nephrin antibodies, each given at a dose too low to cause nephritis on its own. The animals developed proteinuria that did not depend on complement or leukocytes, and their podocyte foot processes were preserved. Podocyte Neph1 and nephrin protein levels fell modestly and ZO-1 protein fell dramatically, with no change in the mRNA levels of any of the 3 genes. The authors concluded that the nephrin-Neph1 interaction appears to be an important determinant of glomerular permeability.
quotes: Disruption of the Neph1-nephrin interaction in vivo by injecting combinations of individual subnephritogenic doses of anti-Neph1 and anti-nephrin results in complement- and leukocyte-independent proteinuria with preserved foot processes.

This disruption modestly reduces Neph1 and nephrin protein expression in podocytes and dramatically reduces ZO-1 protein expression via the interaction of ZO-1 PDZ domains with the cytoplasmic tail of Neph1, independent of changes in mRNA expression of all three genes.
The interaction between nephrin and Neph1 therefore appears to be an important determinant of glomerular permeability.
